readerTitle: Why the threat usually looks worse than you
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (휴대폰 카메라 vs 디지털 카메라) + 실제 연구 (Christensen의 파괴적 혁신 이론, 미니밀 사례) + 가상 사례 (레스토랑, 사내 데이터팀)
insight: 파괴적 위협은 지금의 품질이 아니라 개선 속도와 '이 정도면 충분하다'는 시점으로 판단한다.
misconception: 품질이 떨어지는 싼 경쟁자는 우리 고객이 원하지 않으니 위협이 아니다.

sources.text: Bower, J. L., & Christensen, C. M. (1995). Disruptive Technologies: Catching the Wave. Harvard Business Review.
Christensen, C. M. (1997). The Innovator's Dilemma. Harvard Business School Press. (미니밀 사례 포함)
Christensen, C. M., Raynor, M., & McDonald, R. (2015). What Is Disruptive Innovation? Harvard Business Review.
Lepore, J. (2014). The Disruption Machine. The New Yorker.

factChecks.note: 휴대폰 카메라 사례는 구체 수치 없이 일반적 관찰로만 썼습니다. 초기 휴대폰 카메라의 화질이 낮았고 이후 소형 디지털 카메라 시장이 크게 줄었다는 점은 널리 알려져 있으나, Christensen 본인이 이 사례를 파괴적 혁신으로 분류했는지는 확인하지 않았으므로 카드에서 '패턴'으로만 표현했습니다.
미니밀 사례: 미니밀이 철근(rebar) 같은 저가·저품질 시장에서 시작해 점차 고급 철강 시장으로 올라갔다는 내용은 Christensen(1997) 및 이후 저작에 나옵니다. 연도와 단계별 세부 내용은 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
'파괴적 혁신' 용어는 1995년 HBR 논문(Bower & Christensen)에서 처음 소개되고 1997년 책에서 확장된 것으로 적었습니다. 게시 전 확인하세요.
Jill Lepore(2014, The New Yorker)가 Christensen 이론의 사례 선택과 예측력을 비판했다는 내용을 확인하세요. 카드에는 '사례가 선택적으로 골라졌다는 비판'으로 일반화해 적었습니다.

cards.title: Why the threat usually looks worse than you
body: The first phone cameras took grainy, blurry photos. No photographer took them seriously.
Yet for many people today, the phone is the only camera they own. The thing that won wasn't better at first. It was worse, and it was always in your pocket.

image.label: An old grainy phone photo next to a sharp modern one
image.brief: 왼쪽에 픽셀이 깨진 흐릿한 초기 휴대폰 사진, 오른쪽에 선명한 최신 휴대폰 사진. 가운데 화살표로 시간 흐름 표시. 실제 브랜드 로고나 기기 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A cheaper rival opens down the street.
body: You run a well-reviewed sit-down restaurant. A delivery-only kitchen opens nearby. Its menu is short, the food is fine but plain, and it costs half your prices.
Your regulars say they'd never switch. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore it. Our customers want quality, not cheap food
options.feedback: True today, and that's the trap. You save effort now but miss whether it's getting better fast enough to matter later.

options.text: Cut prices and add a delivery menu to match it
options.feedback: You respond quickly, but you squeeze your margins to fight on its terms before knowing if it's a real threat.

options.text: Watch who buys from it and how fast its food improves
options.feedback: It costs little and tells you what matters: whether it's serving people you ignore, and whether it's closing the gap.

cards.title: Worse, but good enough for new moments.
body: Early phone cameras lost to real cameras on everything photographers cared about: sharpness, zoom, low light.
But they won on something else. They were already with you. People took photos of lunch, receipts and friends, moments nobody carried a camera for.
Then phone cameras improved every year. At some point they became **good enough** for holidays and birthdays too. Camera makers kept serving enthusiasts well, while the mass market moved.

image.label: Everyday moments captured on a phone
image.brief: 일상 장면 콜라주: 점심 접시, 영수증, 친구 셀카를 휴대폰으로 찍는 손. 한쪽 구석에 삼각대 위 큰 카메라가 혼자 서 있음. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Disruptive innovation
body: **Disruptive innovation** is when a product starts out worse on what mainstream customers value, but cheaper, simpler or easier to reach. It wins customers the leaders ignore, then improves until it's good enough for everyone else.

Harvard professor Clayton Christensen introduced the idea in the mid-1990s. His key point: leaders rarely lose by being lazy. They lose by sensibly focusing on their best customers while something 'not good enough' climbs up from below.

image.label: Two lines: leader's product and a rising entrant crossing customer needs
image.brief: 시간축 그래프. 위쪽에 완만히 오르는 점선 "What most customers need", 그 위를 지나가는 "Leader's product" 선, 아래에서 가파르게 올라와 점선을 넘는 "Newcomer" 선. 교차 지점에 "Good enough" 라벨.

cards.title: Steel shows the pattern step by step.
body: In Christensen's research, small 'minimill' steelmakers began with rebar, the cheapest, lowest-quality steel. Big mills were glad to give that business up.
list: **Start where leaders don't care:** low-margin or overlooked customers
**Leaders retreat upward:** dropping that business raises their average margins
**The newcomer improves:** each step up wins the next tier
**Needs rise slowly:** most customers stop paying for 'even better'
cards.callout: The danger isn't where the newcomer is. It's how fast it's moving.

cards.title: Not every new rival is disruptive.
body: A rival that launches a better, pricier product for your best customers is a head-on competitor. Leaders usually win those fights, because they have the money and the customers to respond.

Disruption is different in where it starts. It begins at the bottom of the market, or with people who weren't buying at all. That's why it's so easy to dismiss: by the measures you track, it looks like it's losing.

cards.title: Most cheap entrants stay cheap.
body: Plenty of low-quality newcomers never get good enough and simply fade. Treating every one as a mortal threat can push you into panic moves.

The theory also has critics. Historian Jill Lepore argued in 2014 that its famous cases were selectively chosen. Use it as a lens for spotting a pattern, not as a forecast. The useful test is concrete: is it improving faster than your customers' needs are rising?

cards.title: Now you lead a team inside a big company.
body: Your analytics team builds careful, custom reports for the company. Sales managers start using a cheap self-serve dashboard tool instead. Its numbers are rough, but they get answers in minutes, not weeks.

options.text: Ask IT to block the tool. Its data isn't reliable
options.feedback: You protect accuracy for now, but you push away users who just showed what they value: speed. They'll find another workaround.

options.text: Make your custom reports even more detailed
options.feedback: This pleases your most demanding users, but it moves you further from the managers who wanted 'quick and good enough.'

options.text: Offer a simple self-serve layer yourself, and track what the tool gets good at
options.feedback: You keep deep work for the questions that need it and stop the newcomer from owning everyday questions. It costs some time away from big projects.

cards.title: Judge a rival by its direction, not its quality today.
body: Disruption starts out looking worse. Ask who it serves that you ignore, and how fast it's improving.
**Try it today:** name the cheapest, simplest alternative to what you sell. Write down one thing it couldn't do a year ago that it does now.
